_help.about: §FM.7, §FM.9 (9 Oct). One entry per ruin plant on the compass (data/ruin_compass.json; docs/design/RUIN_ROSTER_REFERENCE.md). Researched by seven parallel agents, one per plant, in PLANT_SCHEMA vocabulary, each passing tools/plant_schema_check.py --strict. San Pedro (data/plants/trichocereus.json) and fly agaric (data/biomes/04_taiga.json) are already in the data and are not repeated here.
_help.sacred: The additive block on each entry. effect_class: visionary, deliriant, stimulant or sedative. rite: one sentence on who used it and for what; rites only, never doses, amounts or preparation (§FM.9). peoples, ruin (an id in ruin_compass.json), conservation (IUCN status), confidence, refs.
_help.flags: Per plant: what the engine can't draw yet (a mushroom, a low globe cactus, a bulb, a twisted vine stem), biome-key gaps, and doubts in the sources. Read before wiring.

_help.egypt: §FP (10 Oct): blue lotus (Nymphaea caerulea) and mandrake (Mandragora officinarum), the Egyptian ruin's two brew plants (Mike, 10 Oct). Written by two parallel agents, one per plant, each passing tools/plant_schema_check.py --strict. Both are 'ground' rosettes as the nearest shape the engine has: neither draws right (a water-lily shape and a trunkless ground rosette are missing; see flags). Evidence is thin for both: blue lotus's sedative effect is only inferred, and mandrake is documented in Egyptian objects and art, not in any ritual text. Mandrake is not native to Egypt (imported in the New Kingdom), and no hot-desert biome key honestly grows either plant: which world holds the Egyptian ruin is open (§FO.9 call 2, §FP.9).
_help.gulf_swamp: Jimsonweed (Datura stramonium), the Gulf South swamp ruin's local psychoactive (10 Oct), added to plants.shrub by one data-fill agent and passing tools/plant_schema_check.py --strict. It sits beside sacred_datura (D. wrightii, a Southwest desert species, unchanged). Evidence is thin: Datura residue (genus only) in Arkansas Mississippian and Caddoan vessels, no named ceremony, and the native range of the species is disputed (see flags). Not yet chosen as the swamp's plant in data/ruin_compass.json.

epiphyte.name: Ipomoea corymbosa

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with the two notched, butterfly-shaped cotyledons of the morning-glory family, then bright green heart-shaped leaves on a thin green twining stem that winds up the nearest shrub. Within a season or two it is a several-metre tangle; the lower stem turns woody and grey-brown while the tips stay green and herbaceous.
growth.source: Habit from Wood et al., Convolvulaceae Unlimited (Turbina corymbosa: liana, twining stems several metres long, woody for most of their length, herbaceous at the tips) and Queensland Biosecurity (scrambling vine to more than 10 m). Germination, growth rate, first flowering and lifespan estimated from related woody Ipomoea.

repro.note: Mass-flowers at the end of the rains into the early dry season (Nov-Feb in Mexico and the Antilles, hence 'Christmas vine'); sweet-scented flowers are a major bee nectar source. Usually one hairy seed per fruit; dried flower clusters with papery sepals persist on the dead stems. Long cultivated, so people carried it far beyond its core range.

epiphyte.source: Ipomoea corymbosa (L.) Roth, syn. Turbina corymbosa (L.) Raf., Rivea corymbosa (L.) Hallier f. Kew POWO: liana, native Mexico (all regions) through Central America, the West Indies and Bahamas to Venezuela, Colombia, Peru, Bolivia, Paraguay and Brazil; introduced Florida, Queensland, Canaries, Old World tropics. Wood et al., Convolvulaceae Unlimited: thorn scrub, thickets, savannas, open woodland, riverbanks, swamps, dry hillsides, mountain and river-valley forest, sea level to 1100 m (exceptionally 1450 m), on granitic, limestone, coral rock, swampy and fertile soils; flowering peaks Nov-Jan in Middle America and the West Indies. Seeds are poisonous (ergoline alkaloids).

stem.notes: twining stems, grey-brown and woody for most of their length, green and herbaceous at the tips; drapes over shrubs and small trees

leaf.notes: heart-shaped, about as wide as long, deep cordate notch with rounded ears, short drawn-out point; on long 4-6 cm stalks; hairless, paler beneath with short white hairs on the main veins

flower.form: white bell-funnel 2.5-3 cm with a dark brown-purple throat, in loose many-flowered branched clusters on long stalks from the leaf axils; whole vine goes white in bloom

fruit.form: small pointed ovoid fruit 1-1.5 cm, beaked, cupped in papery straw-coloured sepals; one hairy brown seed; persists on dead stems

appearance.seasonal: green through the rains; at the turn to the dry season the vine is blanketed in white flowers, then in papery straw-coloured fruit clusters
appearance.silhouette: heart-leaved twining vine blanketing shrubs, white-flowered at dry season
appearance.refs: Wood et al., Convolvulaceae Unlimited (Turbina corymbosa); Flowers of India (Christmas vine: leaves 4-10 x 3-9 cm, ovate-cordate with rounded ears; flowers 2.5-3 cm, funnel-shaped, cream with dark centre; capsules 11-14 x 3-4 mm); Queensland Biosecurity (Turbina): white bell-shaped flowers with a dark brown-purple centre, open morning to evening; Wikipedia Ipomoea corymbosa

bark.note: old stems woody; tips green and herbaceous

fruiting.source: Wood et al., Convolvulaceae Unlimited (corolla campanulate, white with a dark brown to purplish lower tube, 2.5-3 cm; compound cymes on 15-25 cm peduncles; fruit ovoid-oblong 10-15 x 5-6 mm, apiculate, usually one seed 8-11 mm; flowering peaks Nov-Jan in Middle America; flowers an important bee nectar source). Queensland Biosecurity (flowers open in the morning and close in the evening; beaked fruit stays attached to the dead stems). Seeds poisonous. Flowers per cluster, fruit set, ripening, hang, rot and crop estimated.

sacred.rite: Aztec priests and curers took the seeds, called ololiuhqui, to divine the causes of illness, theft and misfortune and to speak with the gods, and Mazatec, Zapotec, Chinantec and Mixe healers in Oaxaca still used them for divination in the twentieth century.
sacred.refs: Hernandez (16th c.) and Sahagun, Florentine Codex, via Schultes 1941, 'A contribution to our knowledge of Rivea corymbosa, the narcotic ololiuqui of the Aztecs' (Harvard Botanical Museum); Wasson 1963, 'Notes on the present status of ololiuhqui and the other hallucinogens of Mexico', Bot. Mus. Leafl. Harvard 20: 161-193; Wikipedia Ipomoea corymbosa and Aztec use of entheogens. Active class: ergolines.

epiphyte.name: Banisteriopsis caapi
epiphyte.synonym: Banisteria caapi; Banisteriopsis inebrians; B. quitensis

growth.juvenile_note: A thin green-brown searching shoot with paired opposite ovate leaves that twines anticlockwise up the nearest stem; within a few years the stem browns and thickens, and older stems coil around each other into a knotted, rope-like twist that climbs into the canopy.
growth.source: Habit from Wikipedia and NTBG Tropical Plant Database (giant twining liana to ~30 m; flowers rarely, seldom sets seed, mainly spreads vegetatively). Germination, growth timing and lifespan estimated; no species growth data recorded.

repro.note: Flowers infrequently and seldom sets seed (NTBG); in the wild it persists and spreads mostly by stems that root where they touch the ground. 'runner' is the nearest clonal value for that. Wind-borne winged samaras when it does fruit.

epiphyte.source: Banisteriopsis caapi (Spruce ex Griseb.) C.V.Morton, Malpighiaceae. Kew POWO: climber of the wet tropical biome, native to NW Argentina, Bolivia, N and W-C Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Venezuela. Wikipedia: giant liana to 30 m twining on other plants; flowers white or pale pink, 12-14 mm, mostly January, infrequently. NTBG Tropical Plant Database: bark chocolate-brown and smooth; leaves opposite, oval, entire, 8-18 x 3.5-8 cm, glabrous above; axillary or terminal cymose panicles; pink petals 5-7 mm; 10 stamens; fruit a samara; flowers rarely. PFAF: moist tropics from about sea level to 1,000 m, rainforest. Range poorly known in the wild (Ermakova 2022, Chacruna).

sacred.rite: Shamans and healers of many western Amazonian peoples (Shipibo-Conibo, Tukano, Cofán, Asháninka) lead night-long sung ceremonies around the vine for healing, divination and meeting the forest spirits.
sacred.refs: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979); Reichel-Dolmatoff, The Shaman and the Jaguar (1975, Tukano); Gebhart-Sayer (1986) and Brabec de Mori (2014) on Shipibo-Conibo icaro healing songs; Luna, Vegetalismo (1986); Spruce's 1852 Vaupés account; Ermakova 2022 (Chacruna) on conservation: not listed or assessed by IUCN.

stem.notes: Woody stem, chocolate-brown and smooth when young, rougher with age; stems twist on themselves and around each other into a knotted, rope- or corkscrew-like cable with knobby swollen nodes, looping from the forest floor up into the crown.

appearance.leaf_notes: Opposite pairs of plain, entire, egg-shaped leaves with a short drawn-out tip, deep matte green above, paler below; pairs held flat along the hanging stems.

flower.form: loose branched sprays of small 5-petalled pale-pink flowers, petals clawed and frilly, at shoot tips and leaf axils

fruit.form: small nut with one broad papery wing (samara), green ripening tan-brown, spinning down on the wind

appearance.seasonal: evergreen; rare flushes of pink flowers early in the wet season
appearance.silhouette: corkscrew-twisted brown cable looping into the canopy, leafy above
appearance.refs: NTBG Tropical Plant Database (Banisteriopsis caapi); Wikipedia; Kew POWO; Top Tropicals catalogue (reddish-brown stem, smooth deep-green oval leaves, pink and white flower clusters); Ark (yaogara.org) species page (stem rugose with age; Indigenous growers tell morphotypes apart by stem relief and bark colour).

epiphyte.silhouette: corkscrew-twisted brown cable looping into the canopy, leafy above

bark.note: Chocolate-brown and smooth (NTBG), rugose on old stems; the twist itself is a stem form, not a bark pattern.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (flowers white or pale pink, 12-14 mm, most often January, infrequent); NTBG (axillary or terminal cymose panicles, pink petals 5-7 mm, fruit a samara, flowers rarely and seldom sets seed). Malpighiaceae flowers are typically worked by oil-collecting bees; samara size, cluster counts, ripening and crop estimated.

ground.name: Psilocybe mexicana

growth.source: Fruiting-body stage lengths estimated for a small fragile Psilocybe; fruits May to October (Wikipedia Psilocybe mexicana).

repro.note: The mycelium is the organism and lives in the grassy soil for years; the mushroom is a days-long fruiting body. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading through the soil; 'wind' = spores. It can form sclerotia (hard underground resting bodies) that carry it through the dry season and fire; 'dormant: dry' stands for them.

ground.source: Psilocybe mexicana R. Heim (Index Fungorum), section Mexicanae; Hymenogastraceae (older works: Strophariaceae). Grows alone or in small groups on soil among moss and short grazed grass in subtropical pastures and humid meadows, on roadsides, trails and cornfield margins, and in grassy places bordering pine-oak and cloud forest, roughly 1000-1800 m, May to October; Guerrero, Michoacan, Morelos, Jalisco, Oaxaca, Veracruz and Puebla to Guatemala (Guzman 1983 monograph via Wikipedia; Guzman in Scientia Fungorum; Redalyc 57404303 'praderas subtropicales con pastos rasantes'). Active compound class: psilocybin. The sacred mushroom of the Mazatec veladas recorded by Heim and Wasson in Huautla de Jimenez.

sacred.rite: Aztec (Mexica) nobles and merchants ate teonanácatl, the 'god mushroom', at feasts and for divination, and Mazatec curanderas such as María Sabina still keep all-night healing vigils (veladas) with it, while Maya use is only reported, from the debated mushroom stones of highland Guatemala.
sacred.refs: Sahagún, Florentine Codex (Aztec teonanácatl at feasts); Wasson & Wasson 1957, Mushrooms, Russia and History, and Heim & Wasson 1958 (Mazatec veladas, María Sabina); Borhegyi on Guatemalan mushroom stones (Maya link reported, debated); Chacruna 2021 'Psychoactive Mushrooms in Mexico' (peoples); Wikipedia Psilocybin mushroom.

cap.form: small conic to bell-shaped cap, often with a low nipple, ochre-brown drying to straw-beige; bruises blue-green
cap.notes: hygrophanous: wet caps are darker brown, drying from the centre to pale straw; faint blue or green tones and blue bruising where handled; no ring on the stem

underside.type: gills grey to purple-brown with whitish edges, adnate to adnexed

appearance.habit: alone or in small groups among moss and short grazed grass on pastures, trail edges and cornfield margins
appearance.seasonal: fruits only in the rainy season (May to October), then rots within days; sclerotia wait out the dry season underground
appearance.silhouette: tiny ochre bell on a tall thread-thin stalk in grass
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Psilocybe mexicana (cap 0.5-2(3) cm, conic to campanulate or subumbonate, ochre to brown, straw in age, blue-bruising; gills grey to purple-brown with whitish edges; stipe 4-10(12.5) cm x 1-2(3) mm, straw to reddish-brown, no annulus; spore print dark purple-brown); Guzman 1983 The Genus Psilocybe

ground.name: Boophone disticha
ground.synonym: Buphane disticha; Boophone toxicaria; Brunsvigia disticha; Haemanthus toxicarius

growth.juvenile_note: The big round seed sends down a root and swells a pea-sized bulb that puts up one or two narrow grey-green straps. Each year the bulb fattens, its brown papery tunics thicken, and the leaves multiply into the two-ranked fan; it does not flower until the bulb is large, about 4-5 years from seed, and grown bulbs sit with their neck and upper half bare above the soil.
growth.source: LLIFLE Boophone disticha (4-5 years seed to flower); PlantZAfrica / SANBI (bulbs do not flower until quite large; slow to flower after moving). Germination and lifespan estimated; common name 'century plant' reflects long-lived bulbs.

repro.note: Flowers at the end of the dry season, often right after a grass fire, before the leaves. Pedicels lengthen into a big spherical seed head that snaps off when dry and rolls across the burnt veld as a tumbleweed, dropping seed. Rarely offsets. Leaves die back in the dry winter.

ground.source: Kew POWO / Flora Zambesiaca (bulbous geophyte, SE South Sudan to South Africa; grassland or wooded grassland on well-drained soils, 200-2,500 m; seasonally dry tropical biome; bulb to 25 cm, partly exposed; leaves grey-green to bluish-green, stiff, to 50-60 cm x 1.5-4.2 cm, after the flowers; scape 5-30 cm; dense head of pink to dark purple flowers; 3-angled capsule, wind-tumbled head). PlantZAfrica / SANBI (dry grassland and rocky slopes, summer-rainfall; fan of erect grey-green leaves; flowers July-October; bees and flies; very poisonous; Declining). LLIFLE (8-16 glaucous leaves, often strongly undulate; hundreds of tunics; flowers after grassland fires). Random Harvest (fire induces flowering; grows on grassland, rocky outcrops, mountainsides). Pacific Bulb Society (wavy-edged grey-green leaves to 45 x 5 cm). Very poisonous to people and stock.

sacred.rite: Zulu, Xhosa, Sotho, Shona and San healers and diviners used the poisonous bulb in divination, to see in vision who or what lay behind a person's misfortune, and in initiation, the Sotho in the boys' initiation lodge (lebollo).
sacred.conservation: not assessed (IUCN); Declining on the Red List of South African Plants (wild harvest for medicine markets)
sacred.refs: Sobiecki J.F. 2008, A review of plants used in divination in southern Africa and their psychoactive effects, Southern African Humanities 20(2): 333-351; Nyazema, Chanyandura & Egan 2024, The use and potential abuse of psychoactive plants in southern Africa: an overview, Frontiers in Pharmacology 15:1269247 (Zulu, Xhosa, Shona and San divination; Sesotho name leshoma); Pasquali 2021, Leshoma, the visionary plant of southern Africa, Antrocom 17(1) (Sotho lebollo initiation); SANBI Red List status.

trunk.notes: the 'stem' is a huge onion-like bulb 15-25 cm across, the top half sitting bare on the ground, wrapped in hundreds of brown papery tunics that fray into a shaggy neck

leaf.notes: 8-16 stiff, blunt, glaucous grey-green straps in two ranks, a flat upright fan (often twisted) in ONE plane from the bulb neck; edges strongly rippled

flower.form: a single dense round head 15-30 cm of 50-200 narrow pink-to-red trumpets with long protruding stamens and yellow anthers, on a short thick stalk that seems to sit on the bulb; no leaves yet

fruit.form: pedicels stretch to ~30 cm into a big straw-coloured spoked sphere tipped with 3-angled capsules; it snaps off and rolls as a tumbleweed

appearance.seasonal: deciduous geophyte: bare bulb in the dry season, pink ball after the first fire or rains, then the grey fan of leaves through the wet summer; fan yellows and dies back in autumn
appearance.silhouette: grey-green strap fan in one plane on a bare brown bulb
appearance.refs: Kew POWO / Flora Zambesiaca; PlantZAfrica (SANBI); LLIFLE; Pacific Bulb Society wiki; Wikipedia Boophone disticha; Random Harvest

bark.note: the exposed bulb: many layers of thin brown tunics, paler cream where they tear

fruiting.source: PlantZAfrica (flowers July-October; bees and flies); Kew POWO / FZ (10-200+ flowers in a ball; 3-angled capsule to 3-4 cm; pedicels lengthen in fruit); Wikipedia (about fifty flowers; pedicels to ~30 cm; head becomes a tumbleweed). 'falls' here means the whole dry head breaks off and rolls. Flower days, fruit set, ripening and crop estimated.

ground.name: Lophophora williamsii
ground.silhouette: flat blue-green button with woolly tufts, flush with the ground

growth.juvenile_note: Two tiny cotyledons, then a pea-sized grey-green globe with five ribs and tufts of white wool, usually in leaf litter under a nurse shrub. It widens far more than it rises, adding ribs in Fibonacci steps (5, then 8, then 13) as it ages, the crown staying flat or slightly domed with a woolly centre and the body pulled down into a long carrot-like taproot. Growth facts: in the wild it is very slow, taking roughly 10 to 30 years from seed to flowering size (3 to 10 in cultivation). A crown cut off above the root leaves the buried stem alive, and that stem sends up new heads (pups) from its buried areoles; a cut into the root kills the plant, because roots cannot make new crowns. Regrown heads come back smaller and more numerous (2.6 crowns per plant two years after one harvest, against 1.7 uncut) and need well over six years, probably eight or more, to reach flowering size again.
growth.source: Llifle encyclopedia (very slow; wild plants up to 30 years to flower, cultivated 6-10; taproot 25 cm+); United Plant Savers (3-15 years to reproductive maturity; Terry 2017 IUCN); Chacruna harvesting guidelines (seedlings 5-ribbed, >10 years to mature from seed; six years not enough to regenerate, eight likely the minimum); Trout & Norton 2011, Erowid Extracts 20 (new crowns from the subterranean stem; 2.6 vs 1.7 crowns after two years); Cactus Conservation Institute (cut too low and no new stems form). Germination and lifespan estimated.

repro.note: Solitary or clustering; damaged or cut crowns put up new heads from the buried stem, so old plants and harvested ground show tight clumps of small buttons. Flowers open by day from the woolly crown centre.

ground.source: Small spineless button cactus of the Chihuahuan Desert scrub and the Tamaulipan thorn scrub of south Texas and north-central to north-east Mexico (Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León, Tamaulipas, San Luis Potosí, Zacatecas), 100-1,900 m, on calcareous (limestone) gravelly clay and loam soils, rocky slopes and dry riverbeds, usually under nurse shrubs (cenizo Leucophyllum, Acacia, creosote bush Larrea, tasajillo Opuntia leptocaulis, lechuguilla). Stem 2-7 cm tall, 4-12 cm wide, flattened, blue-green to grey-green, 5-13 rounded ribs, areoles with tufts of white to yellowish wool, no spines; most of the plant is a buried stem and a 25 cm+ taproot. Pink to whitish bell flowers 1.5-2.5 cm from the crown centre, March-May and sporadically to September; club-shaped pink fruit to 2 cm, drying brownish-white. Wikipedia Peyote; Llifle; Kew POWO; Cactus Conservation Institute; Ermakova et al. 2020; sacredcacti.com associated flora (citing Anderson 1980).

sacred.rite: The Wixárika (Huichol) walk a yearly pilgrimage to the desert of Wirikuta in San Luis Potosí to gather peyote as the sacrament of their deities, and the Native American Church holds it as the sacrament of its all-night prayer and healing meetings.
sacred.conservation: IUCN Vulnerable (Terry 2013, amended 2017), declining: wild crowns overharvested (often cut too deep to regrow) and habitat lost to clearing for grazing, farms and border-town growth; under special protection (Pr) in Mexico.
sacred.refs: Wikipedia Peyote (Wixárika sacrament; Native American Church all-night ceremonies; IUCN Vulnerable); United Plant Savers (Terry 2017 IUCN assessment, threats, Mexican protection); Cactus Conservation Institute; Ermakova et al. 2020, bioRxiv 10.1101/2020.04.03.023515 (harvest and habitat conversion). Active compound class: mescaline.

traits.native_range: Chihuahuan Desert and Tamaulipan thorn scrub, Mexico and south Texas
traits.leaf_shape: none — woolly areoles on ribs, no spines
traits.trunk: succulent flattened globe, mostly below ground
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

stem.notes: Peyote: a flat, blue-green, matte button sunk to its rim in gravel; broad low ribs cut into rounded bumps by cross-furrows, each bump topped with a white wool tuft and NO spines; the centre is a dense white woolly boss. Often in tight clumps of several heads under a grey shrub.

flower.form: small pink-and-white bell 1.5-2.5 cm sitting in the woolly crown centre, open by day

fruit.form: small pink club-shaped berry to 2 cm poking out of the wool, drying brownish-white

appearance.seasonal: evergreen succulent; shrinks and greys, sinking lower into the soil in drought; flowers in spring after rain
appearance.silhouette: flat blue-green button with woolly tufts, flush with the ground
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Peyote; Llifle Lophophora williamsii; Cactus Conservation Institute; Kew POWO

bark.note: spineless: the 'spiny' pattern stands for the areoles, each a white wool tuft on a rounded tubercle

fruiting.source: Wikipedia Peyote (flowers pink or white to yellowish, 1-2.4 cm, open by day, March-May and sometimes to September; fruit club-shaped, fleshy, pink, 1.5-2 cm, drying brownish-white, not bursting, described as edible); Llifle (solitary bell flowers 1.5-2.5 cm from the woolly centre; fruit red to pinkish to 2 cm). Pollinators, fruit set, ripening, hang and crop estimated.

ground.name: Nymphaea caerulea
ground.synonym: Nymphaea nouchali var. caerulea (Savigny) Verdc. (Kew POWO's accepted name); Nymphaea capensis in some treatments
ground.silhouette: flat round pads on still water, blue star flowers above

growth.juvenile_note: The seedling sends up small submerged leaves first, then floating blades on lengthening stalks; the rhizome thickens and the plant spreads to about a metre across, older leaves being pushed to the edge as the stalks lengthen.
growth.source: Wikipedia Nymphaea caerulea (leaves polymorphic, differing underwater and floating; one plant spreads about 1 m; petioles lengthen with age, pushing older leaves outward); Kew POWO (rhizomatous hydrogeophyte). Germination days, years to size and flower, and lifespan are estimates; no source opened gives them. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nymphaea_caerulea ; https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:955147-1

repro.note: A rhizomatous water plant (Kew POWO calls it a hydrogeophyte). Each flower rises over 2-3 days, opens in mid-morning, shuts near dusk and lasts about four days (Wikipedia); the closing is what made it a sun symbol in Egypt. Insect pollination, water dispersal and the bloom season are estimated from the genus, not read in the sources opened.

sacred.rite: Ancient Egyptians made the blue water lily the flower of the sun's daily rebirth (the god Nefertem, 'Water-Lily of the Sun', rises from it) and laid its petals with the dead, as in Tutankhamun's burial, while its use as a mild sedative or intoxicant in festivals such as Hathor's Festival of Drunkenness is only inferred from tomb art, a few texts and modern pharmacology, and is not proven.
sacred.conservation: not evaluated (IUCN); least concern in South Africa (SANBI, per Wikipedia); Wikipedia also calls it rare in Egypt since the Aswan Dam, unverified and in conflict with the SANBI rating
sacred.refs: Wikipedia Nymphaea caerulea (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nymphaea_caerulea): synonymy and range, flower and leaf, sun symbolism, petals in Tutankhamun's burial chamber, and the cautions that the active constituents are unknown, that the alkaloids proposed in the 1970s-80s were not confirmed by later phytochemical work, and that ancient-use claims rest on 'it has been suggested'; Kew POWO (https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:955147-1): accepted as N. nouchali var. caerulea, native range Egypt to southern Africa, rhizomatous hydrogeophyte; UC Berkeley Arts & Humanities, 'Investigating the psychedelic blue lotus of Egypt' (https://artshumanities.berkeley.edu/node/865): petals on Tutankhamun's body, McEvoy's reading of the Hathoric Festival of Drunkenness as reported not verified, the 'scholars have long hypothesized' wine idea as a working hypothesis only, a small comparison of nuciferine in verified versus shop-bought flowers, and the criticism of the 1998 BBC trial and of 'pseudoscience' in the marketing; Wikipedia Nefertem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nefertem): the lotus at creation, the blue water lily and the sun, 'Water-Lily of the Sun'. The Egyptian psychoactive claim is thin evidence and should be read as a probable, not a certain, rite.

ground.source: Nymphaea caerulea (Nymphaea nouchali var. caerulea), Egyptian blue lotus: a rhizomatous floating-leaved water plant of rivers, lakes and pools, native along the Nile and through central, East and southern Africa and the south Arabian peninsula (Yemen, Oman) and the Comoros, recorded from about 10 to 1,650 m in South Africa; it tolerates anoxic mud and nutrient-poor water and can dominate deeper water. Kew POWO lists the native range as Egypt to southern Africa, the southern Arabian peninsula and the Comoros, including Palestine. Flowers 8-12 cm, 14-20 petals, pale bluish-white to sky-blue or mauve with a pale yellow centre, opening mid-morning and shutting near dusk; leaves 8-35 cm, round with an incised notch, margin entire near the tip or wavy. Ceremonial use: sun and creation symbol, linked to Nefertem, petals in Tutankhamun's burial; the psychoactive use is inferred, not shown. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nymphaea_caerulea ; https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:955147-1 ; https://artshumanities.berkeley.edu/node/865 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nefertem . Temperature band, height, density and soil are estimated.

flower.form: star-shaped water lily 8-12 cm across, 14-20 narrow pointed violet-blue petals (sky-blue to mauve, fading paler toward the base) around a heap of yellow stamens, four green sepals under it, held on its own stalk just above the water; opens mid-morning, shuts near dusk, lasts about four days
flower.notes: Plain petals, no glow. The yellow centre is the one warm spot and the blue is a touch lighter than the water; a bud rises over two or three days, so some flowers stand shut and some open. Opening by morning light and closing at dusk is the whole sun symbolism.

leaf.notes: flat round to slightly oval pads floating on the surface, each with a narrow wedge-shaped notch to the stalk and a faintly pointed tip; smooth above, raised green veins beneath (rarely purplish); edge entire near the tip or wavy

stem.notes: thick, spongy, blackish-green leaf and flower stalks run down into the mud; nothing stands above the water but the flowers

fruit.form: rounded spongy fruit that ripens under water; not drawn (estimated from the genus)

appearance.seasonal: flowers through the warm months; the sources opened give May to October for India only
appearance.silhouette: flat round pads on still water, blue star flowers above
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Nymphaea caerulea (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nymphaea_caerulea): flower size, petal count and colour, leaf size and shape, sepals, opening and closing; Kew POWO (https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:955147-1). Fruit form estimated.

Months for Egypt, pollinators, fruit kind, size and timings, and crop are estimated from the genus; no source opened covers them. edible 'no' is about the fruit only and says nothing about the rhizome or seeds. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nymphaea_caerulea

ground.name: Mandragora officinarum
ground.silhouette: flat dark-green wrinkled leaf rosette, purple bells at centre

growth.juvenile_note: A few small oval leaves lie flat on the ground from a thread of root that thickens into a carrot-like taproot, often forking in two (up to about 1.2 m long in an old plant). Each year of the cool wet season the rosette is bigger, its leaves broader and more blistered, and in the hot dry summer it dies back to the root and sleeps until the autumn rains. Only a large rosette sets flowers, from the centre.
growth.source: Root form, summer die-back and the cool-season growing season from PFAF (https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Mandragora+officinarum: deep, often branched taproot up to 1.2 m, often divides in two; dies back to its roots in hot dry summers and grows in mild moist winters) and Cretan Flora (flowers Nov/Jan to early April). Germination time, years to size, age at first flowering and lifespan are estimated; no source opened gives them.

repro.note: Flowers in the cool wet season (November to April; the bloom.season 'spring' is the nearest value to that), then the round fruit ripens into early summer and the leaves die back to the taproot for the hot dry months. No clonal spread; the root forks but the plant stays a single crown. Pollinators and dispersers are estimated, not documented.

toxic.effect: deliriant (tropane alkaloids: hyoscyamine, atropine, scopolamine); every part is poisonous, the root most of all: never eaten, never browsed

sacred.rite: New Kingdom Egyptians, from the 18th Dynasty, held and exchanged the imported mandrake fruit at banquets and wore, carried and buried it as a charm of love, fertility and renewal, though no surviving text sets out a ritual for it.
sacred.conservation: Endangered on the IUCN Europe regional assessment (Bilz & Soljan 2011, as quoted by Wikipedia); no global assessment found

ground.source: Mandragora officinarum L., Solanaceae, a stemless perennial from a thick, often forked taproot. RANGE: Kew POWO accepts the species narrowly, native N Italy to the NW Balkan Peninsula (the page's list also names Lebanon-Syria, and the page contradicts itself on this) (https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:816733-1), and gives the wider Mediterranean range from Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia through Iberia, Italy, Greece and Turkey to Lebanon-Syria and Palestine to the autumn-flowering M. autumnalis (https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:816721-1); Wikipedia keeps the broad sense, native around the Mediterranean in N Africa, S Iberia, Italy, the former Yugoslavia, Greece, Cyprus, S Turkey and the Levant (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandragora_officinarum; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandrake_(plant)). Egypt is in neither list. HABITAT: open, often disturbed ground: light woodland, olive groves, fallow land, waysides, railway embankments and ruins, sea level to 1,200 m (Wikipedia; PFAF https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Mandragora+officinarum); rocky flats and slopes with dry open shrubby vegetation, open grassy places, fallow terraces, waste ground and archaeological sites, 0-700 m and occasionally to 1,200 m on Crete (Cretan Flora https://www.cretanflora.com/mandragora_officinarum_text.html). PFAF: prefers deep, humus-rich, light, circumneutral soil, roots rot in wet or poorly draining ground, dies back to the root in hot dry summers and grows in mild moist winters, hardy to about -15 C for short spells if well drained. FORM: leaves in a basal rosette, usually spreading flat on the ground, ovate-elliptic, 12-20 cm (Cretan Flora; RHS https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/10849/mandragora-officinarum/details gives dark green leaves to 30 cm; Wikipedia up to 45 cm and variable), entire or irregularly sinuate-lobed, bullate (blistered), nearly hairless, indistinct stalk; bell flowers 2-4 cm from the centre of the rosette, greenish-white to blue-violet, on slender stalks shorter than the leaves, November/January to April (Cretan Flora; Wikipedia says September to April; RHS: greenish-white with purple staining); round to ellipsoid berry 5-40 mm, ripening glossy yellow to orange from November to June; a long thick root. TOXICITY: all parts poisonous, tropane alkaloids including hyoscyamine, atropine and scopolamine (Wikipedia; Kew Adopt-a-seed https://adoptaseed.kew.org/seed/mandrake.html). EGYPT: not native; the plant reached Egypt in the New Kingdom, probably from Canaan and the Levant, and had to be planted and irrigated (https://www.ucm.es/data/cont/docs/621-2017-06-23-El%20fruto%20del%20deseo.pdf; https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228634623_Herbal_medicine_in_ancient_Egypt; https://egypt-museum.com/mandrake-and-lotus-broad-collar/). Taxonomy caveat: whether the Egyptian plant and the western Mediterranean plant are M. officinarum or M. autumnalis is unsettled (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandragora_(genus)).

trunk.notes: stemless: no trunk above ground. Below ground a thick, pale carrot-like taproot, often forked in two, up to about 1.2 m long, which is where the plant's lore comes from; the rosette sits flat on bare soil.

leaf.notes: large ovate-elliptic leaves, dark green and blistered (bullate: the surface puckers between the veins), edge entire to shallowly wavy-lobed, nearly hairless, the stalk short and hardly separate from the blade; upright when young, then spread flat on the ground in a wheel. Dark-green colour from RHS, blistering from Cretan Flora.

flower.form: broad upright bells 2-4 cm with five short triangular lobes, greenish-white shading to violet or purple, on slender stalks shorter than the leaves so they nestle in the centre of the rosette; a tuft of long narrow green sepals under each

fruit.form: round to egg-shaped berry 2.5-4 cm in the middle of the leaf wheel, green then glossy yellow to orange like a small tomato or apple, with a strong apple-like scent; poisonous

appearance.seasonal: leaves come with the autumn rains and lie flat through the mild wet winter; bells in the centre from about November to April; round yellow-orange fruit through spring and early summer; the whole rosette withers to the root in the hot dry summer
appearance.silhouette: flat dark-green wrinkled leaf rosette, purple bells at centre
appearance.refs: Cretan Flora https://www.cretanflora.com/mandragora_officinarum_text.html (leaves flat on the ground, ovate-elliptic, bullate, subglabrous, 12-20 cm; flowers violet or purple 30-40 mm; berry yellow or orange); RHS https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/10849/mandragora-officinarum/details (dark green rosette leaves to 30 cm, greenish-white flowers with purple staining, yellow fruit, stemless); Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandragora_officinarum; PFAF https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Mandragora+officinarum. Flower stalk length, calyx and fruit scent are from Cretan Flora and PFAF.

bark.note: stemless: there is no stem to draw. green_stem stands for the short leaf stalks at the crown (color) and the pale-brown taproot top where it meets the soil (color_2).

fruiting.source: Cretan Flora https://www.cretanflora.com/mandragora_officinarum_text.html (bells 30-40 mm from the rosette centre on 2-8 cm stalks, November/January to April; berry 25-30 mm yellow or orange); Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandragora_officinarum (flowers September to April, berry 5-40 mm ripening November to June, glossy yellow to orange); PFAF https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Mandragora+officinarum (strong apple-like scent; fruit possibly poisonous). Pollinators, flowers per plant, fruit set, ripening, hang and rot times and crop are estimated. A bud-to-fruit span of months is why ripen_days is long.

shrub.name: Erythroxylum coca
shrub.origin: Eastern Andes of Peru and Bolivia
shrub.synonym: Erythroxylum coca var. coca (Huánuco or Bolivian coca)

growth.juvenile_note: A thin single-stemmed seedling with a few small bright-green elliptic leaves, traditionally raised in shaded seedbeds; it branches from low down within a year or two into a twiggy, upright shrub of slender reddish-brown stems with leaves set flat along the side shoots.
growth.source: Wikipedia Coca (seed sown in shaded seedbeds; var. coca cuttings do not root easily); Encyclopedia.com Coca (leaves picked from 6-12 months after planting; plants productive 30-40 years); FAO Ecocrop E. coca (1-3 years to first harvest, ~20 years economic life). Germination days and height years estimated.

repro.note: Flowers heterostylous (two style forms on different plants; Ganders 1979, Bohm, Ganders and Plowman 1982). Var. coca is propagated by seed; its cuttings root poorly, unlike the Amazonian var. ipadu. Red drupes taken by birds (estimated).

shrub.source: Erythroxylum coca var. coca, Huánuco or Bolivian coca: evergreen shrub 1-3 m (to ~5 m unpruned), reddish-brown bark, light-green elliptic leaves 4-8 cm with two arching lines either side of the midrib beneath, small yellowish-white five-petalled flowers in axillary clusters, red-orange ovoid drupes. Grown on the humid eastern slopes of the Andes of Peru and Bolivia (yungas montane forest, about 1000-2000 m; down to ~500 m in the premontane belt), frost-tender, on very acid soils. Known almost only in cultivation; genomic work (White et al. 2020) derives it from the wild E. gracilipes, domesticated in southeastern Peru. Wikipedia Coca and Erythroxylum coca; Sauvain et al. 1997 J. Ethnopharmacol. 56; Sayre (USP VIII) leaf description; Plowman 1984.

sacred.rite: Quechua and Aymara peoples offer coca leaves to the apus (mountain spirits), Inti and Pachamama, read them in divination and chew them together in acullico; under the Inca coca was a sacred, state-controlled plant of priests and nobles, used in offerings and divination and placed with the dead.
sacred.refs: Wikipedia Coca (religious use: offerings to the apus, Inti and Pachamama; divination; Inca state monopoly; leaves placed with mummies); Encyclopedia.com Coca (sacred under the Inca, reserved to chieftains, priests and privileged classes; leaves buried with the dead). The leaf is not the refined drug.

traits.native_range: Eastern Andean slopes of Peru and Bolivia (yungas), 500-2000 m; known mainly in cultivation
traits.leaf_shape: small glossy elliptic leaves with two arching lines beneath
traits.trunk: multi-stemmed from the base, slender reddish-brown stems
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

bark.notes: thin smooth red-brown stems with pale lenticel dots; twigs set with small brown persistent stipule scales

leaf.notes: bright light-green, slightly glossy, thin-leathery ellipses on very short stalks; beneath, two pale curved lines run from base to tip either side of the midrib, enclosing a narrow leaf-shaped panel: the species' tell at close range

flower.form: tiny yellowish-white five-petalled stars, under 1 cm, in little clusters on short stalks in the leaf axils and along older twigs

fruit.form: small ovoid scarlet to red-orange drupes, about 1 cm, scattered along the twigs like beads

appearance.seasonal: evergreen; flushes of bright new leaves after the rains; red drupes after flowering
appearance.silhouette: upright twiggy shrub of flat bright-green leaf sprays
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Coca; Sauvain et al. 1997 (shrub 1-2 m, leaves to ~8 x 5 cm, white or yellowish flowers, red-orange drupe); Sayre, USP VIII Coca (Huánuco leaf 2.5-7.5 cm, nearly elliptical, short point, entire, smooth and slightly glossy, two lines beneath); Naturalis Useful Plants (reddish-brown bark, light green leaves to 7 cm)

shrub.silhouette: upright twiggy shrub of flat bright-green leaf sprays

bark.note: Erythroxylum: 'red wood'; reddish-brown bark (Naturalis Useful Plants); lenticels on the branches (PROSEA, for the sister species)

fruiting.source: Wikipedia Coca (small yellowish-white five-petalled flowers in clusters on short stalks; red berries); Sauvain et al. 1997 (red-orange oblong to ovate drupe); PROSEA E. novogranatense (petals ~4 mm, 1-4(-8) per cluster, heterodistylous). Season, pollinators, fruit size, timings and counts estimated.

shrub.name: Datura wrightii

growth.juvenile_note: Seed lies dormant in sandy wash soil for years and comes up after warm-season rain or disturbance. Two narrow cotyledons, then soft, dull grey-green, hairy ovate leaves on a stout stem that forks early; growth is very fast and a first-year plant can already be a low sprawling mound with a few white trumpets. It builds a fleshy tuberous root, dies back to the ground after frost and resprouts each warm season into a wider mound.
growth.source: Arizona Cooperative Extension 'Sacred Datura' (fleshy tuberous root, dies back after freezes and resprouts; 2-3 ft tall, sprawling 6-8 ft); UW ESRM 412 propagation protocol DAWR2 (seed dormant in soil for decades, germinates in warm moist months, very rapid early growth, can flower at 2-5 weeks; short-lived perennial in warm climates, annual in the cold north of its range). Germination window and lifespan estimated.

repro.note: Each trumpet opens at dusk and closes by the next late morning or noon; hawkmoths (Manduca) pollinate it at night, bees visit in the early morning. The nodding capsule bursts irregularly and drops its light-brown seed under the plant, where wash floods carry it on. The tuberous root resprouts the same plant each year; it does not spread clonally.

toxic.effect: deliriant (tropane alkaloids); every part is deadly poisonous: never eaten, never browsed

sacred.rite: Zuni rain priests used it in rites to bring rain and in divination, and the Chumash, Tongva, Luiseño and Kumeyaay of southern California gave it in toloache initiation rites marking a youth's passage to adulthood and in shamans' vision rites; it is deadly poisonous and not every initiate survived.
sacred.refs: Stevenson 1915, Ethnobotany of the Zuni Indians (BAE 30th Annual Report), pp. 46, 48, 88 (use restricted to the rain priests and the directors of the Little Fire and Cimex fraternities; rain and divination); Applegate 1975, The Datura cult among the Chumash (J. California Anthropology 2); Robinson et al. 2020, PNAS 117(49), Datura quids at Pinwheel Cave, Chumash-area rock art site, AD 1530-1890; Du Bois 1908, The Religion of the Luiseño Indians of Southern California; Garcia & Adams 2005, Healing with Medicinal Plants of the West (Chumash momoy, Tongva manit); Wikipedia Datura wrightii; Southwest Desert Flora (Diegueño toloache initiation)

shrub.source: Datura wrightii, sacred datura - sprawling, grey-green, densely appressed-hairy herbaceous perennial from a tuberous root, 0.3-1.5 m tall and up to 2.4 m wide, of open sandy or gravelly ground: desert washes and arroyos, canyon floors, roadsides and other periodically disturbed places, in creosote and Joshua-tree desert scrub, desert grassland, sagebrush and pinyon-juniper, and California coastal and foothill scrub, from sea level to about 2,200 m (7,200 ft). Native from California, Nevada, Utah and Colorado through Arizona, New Mexico and Texas into northern Mexico and Baja California; most abundant in southern California (Wikipedia; Arizona Cooperative Extension; Native Plant Society of New Mexico; Southwest Desert Flora; UW ESRM 412 protocol DAWR2; birdandhike.com). Kew POWO (Datura wrightii Regel, accepted) gives a narrower native range, S Central USA to N Mexico. Deliriant (tropane alkaloids); every part is deadly poisonous. Ceremonial use documented: Zuni rain and divination rites, southern California toloache initiation.

flower.form: huge upright white trumpet 15-20 cm long, flaring to a 10 cm five-pointed rim, the points drawn out into thin threads, rim sometimes faintly violet; one in each fork of the stems, open from dusk to mid-morning, a limp twisted white rag by afternoon
flower.notes: Plain white petals lit only by moon or torch; they do NOT glow. Brightest white in the scrub at night because they are white, not because they give off light.

fruit.form: round spiny capsule 3-4 cm, nodding on a curved stalk below the stem, densely covered in slender short spines; turns tan and bursts irregularly, spilling light-brown seeds

appearance.seasonal: dies back to the ground after frost and resprouts from the root each warm season; flowers April to October, new trumpets each evening
appearance.silhouette: low sprawling grey-green mound with big upturned white trumpets
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Datura wrightii; Native Plant Society of New Mexico Wildflowers of New Mexico (blades 2.5-10 in, entire to wavy or coarsely toothed; flowers 6-10 in, petal tips with slender threads; round 1 in capsule densely short-spiny, hanging down); Southwest Desert Flora (white to pale lavender, nodding globose capsule bursting irregularly, spines under 1/3 in, seeds light brown); Arizona Cooperative Extension (leaves grey-green below, flowers open early evening, close by noon); americansouthwest.net

bark.note: stout herbaceous stems dulled grey-green by dense flat-lying hairs; darker at the forks

architecture.note: sympodial forking in twos at every node with a single flower in the fork (the Datura pattern); low stems sprawl outward and lie half on the ground, so the plant is wider than tall

fruiting.source: Wikipedia Datura wrightii (white trumpets to 20 cm, blooms April-October, open morning and evening, spiny globular capsule 3-4 cm opening when ripe); Arizona Cooperative Extension (dozens of flowers per plant, opening early evening, closing by noon; hawkmoth pollinated). Fruit set, ripening, hang and rot times and crop estimated.

shrub.name: Datura stramonium
shrub.silhouette: forking green annual, white trumpets, upright spiny pods

growth.juvenile_note: An annual that comes up from seed in early summer on ground that has been turned, cleared or flooded; the seed can lie in the soil for years. It grows into an erect, freely branching, forking herb and is killed by the first frost. The seedling's own look is not described in any source opened; it is drawn as a small forking sprig like the other Datura.
growth.source: PlantPono Datura stramonium sheet quoting Holm et al. 1997 ('germinates in the field in early summer and flowers from summer through autumn', 'requires disturbed sites for establishment', about 90% germination after 17 years' burial per Burnside et al. 1996, viable in soil up to 40 years per Weber 2017) and PROTA (germination starts after about 2 weeks and is complete after one month); Wikipedia Datura stramonium (annual, frost-sensitive, seed dormant for years until the soil is disturbed); NC State Extension (sensitive to frost). Growth times to half and full height, first seed, lifespan and shade tolerance estimated.

repro.note: A seed-only annual (Holm: 'dispersal is almost wholly by seed'). Each trumpet opens in the evening and has wilted by the next day. PROTA reports hawkmoth pollination and says the plant is largely self-fertile; Wikipedia says nocturnal moths feed on it. repro.pollinator is 'insect' because 'moth' is not used in repro anywhere in the data (fruiting.pollinators carries 'moth' and 'self'). Weber 2017 (via PlantPono): seeds and capsules float on water, so floods carry them along a river bank. 'dormant: cold' stands for the dead plant at the first frost and the seed that waits in the soil; the plant itself does not overwinter.

toxic.effect: deliriant (tropane alkaloids); every part is poisonous: never eaten, never browsed

sacred.rite: Datura residue (not identified to species) is found in Mississippian and Caddoan bottles, bowls and effigy vessels from Arkansas dated about AD 1400-1700, among them a female effigy bottle that its authors tie to the earth-mother figure Old-Woman-Who-Never-Dies, and the authors read the vessels as holding a ritual drink; it is poisonous in every part, the vessels' find places are poorly recorded, and no named people or ceremony is attached.
peoples: Mississippian and Caddoan peoples of Arkansas (archaeological residue only, no named nation)
sacred.conservation: IUCN status not checked; NatureServe global rank GU (unrankable) per the Tennessee-Kentucky Plant Atlas; introduced weed across much of the world (Kew POWO)
sacred.refs: King, Powis, Cheong, Deere, Pickering, Singleton & Gaikwad 2018, Absorbed Residue Evidence for Prehistoric Datura Use in the American Southeast and Western Mexico, Advances in Archaeological Practice 6(4):312-327, doi 10.1017/aap.2018.30 (https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/BC403850B55D372801DE729BB23EAD7D/core-reader; read all but the last 210 characters): atropine found in 13 pottery and 14 shell vessels from the Gilcrease Museum, 7 of 31 Mississippian pottery vessels positive, among them bottles, bowls, a female effigy bottle and a human-head effigy bottle; the authors read the use as ritual; Lambert, Perttula & Gaikwad 2022 (online 2021), Production Matters: Organic Residue Evidence for Late Precolumbian Datura-Making in the Central Arkansas River Valley, Advances in Archaeological Practice 10(2):149-159, doi 10.1017/aap.2021.15 (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/advances-in-archaeological-practice/article/abs/production-matters/8767998261B84066BA893CAF80133288; abstract page only, the full text could not be opened): Datura residues in two Late Precolumbian composite bottles from the Central Arkansas River valley, unlike most Mississippian bottles

shrub.source: Datura stramonium, jimsonweed (thorn apple, Jamestown weed) - erect, freely branching, forking annual herb 0.6-1.5 m tall (Wikipedia 60-150 cm; NC State Extension 1-4 ft; PROTA up to 2 m), with large ovate coarsely toothed leaves, a white (sometimes violet-tinged) evening-opening trumpet and an erect, spiny, four-valved capsule. A weed of disturbed ground, rich moist soil and the places floods and people open up: fields, pastures, roadsides and waste ground, and, in the USGS PlantID and Kansas Wildflowers accounts, floodplains, bottomlands and the banks of streams; annual and killed by frost. Naturalized across the eastern United States; the native range is not settled: Kew POWO lists only Mexico as native and every US state as introduced, bplant.org says 'the exact native range of this species is not known', Weakley's Flora gives 'non-native? presumably introduced from Mexico or Central America' before 1492, the Tennessee-Kentucky Plant Atlas says not native, the Kansas Wildflowers account says native, and King et al. 2018 say its natural range 'is difficult to determine because it has become so widespread'. Deliriant (tropane alkaloids); every part is poisonous. Ritual use is reported only from archaeological residue in Arkansas.

flower.form: upright white trumpet 6-9 cm (Wikipedia; Radford, Ahles & Bell give 7-10 cm), sometimes violet-tinged or with a purple throat, flaring into five lobes each drawn out to a long sharp tooth, held on a long angled green calyx; one at a time in the forks of the stems, open in the evening and wilted the next day
flower.notes: Plain white petals lit only by moon or torch; they do NOT glow. Wikipedia calls the flowers fragrant; 'sweet' is the nearest scent value.

fruit.form: erect egg-shaped capsule 2.5-5 cm, covered in many slender spines, standing up from the fork (not nodding like Datura wrightii's); ripens to light yellow-brown and splits into four valves, spilling black seeds

appearance.seasonal: comes up in early summer, flowers through summer into autumn, ripe fruit until frost; the first frost kills the whole plant and the seed waits in the soil
appearance.silhouette: forking green annual, white trumpets, upright spiny pods
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Datura stramonium (leaves 8-20 cm toothed and undulate, darker above and paler below; trumpets 6-9 cm white, cream or violet; capsule spiny or smooth, splits into four chambers of black seeds); NC State Extension (leaves ovate to oblong-elliptical, hairless, wavy margin with coarse teeth; flowers trumpet-shaped, white to purple-tinged, open only in the evening and wilt the next day; spiked capsule ripens light yellow-brown and splits into 4 valves); namethatplant.net quoting Radford, Ahles & Bell 1968 (funnelform corolla 7-10 cm, 'capsule erect, subglobose or ovoid, 2.5-4cm long, spinose, valvate') and Smith 1998 (ovate leaves with large, coarse, angular teeth); Kansas Wildflowers (capsule 1.4-2 in, many slender spines, four valves); King's American Dispensatory via henriettes-herb.com (stem much branched and forked, yellowish-green; leaves unequal at the base, deeply toothed and sinuate; flowers erect)

bark.note: smooth, branched, yellowish-green herbaceous stem (King's American Dispensatory); darker at the forks. Colours are estimated from that description.

architecture.note: an annual herb, so no woody skeleton; forking in twos at the nodes ('much branched and forked', King's American Dispensatory), the Datura pattern, upright rather than sprawling. Order count, angles and spacing estimated.

fruiting.source: Holm et al. 1997 via PlantPono (flowers May to September in the north temperate zone, ripe fruit from August until frost in November; up to 25,000 seeds per well-nourished plant); NC State Extension (flowers July to September); USGS PlantID (July to October); Wikipedia Datura stramonium (flowers throughout the summer; trumpets 6-9 cm; capsule 3-8 cm); Radford, Ahles & Bell 1968 (capsule 2.5-4 cm). Month range is the span of the sources. Fruit set, ripening, hang and rot times and crop per plant estimated; fruit_size_cm spans Radford and Kansas Wildflowers.

ololiuhqui: Category 'epiphyte' follows most existing liana entries (Ivy, Passion vine, Monstera); the vine is rooted in the ground, not epiphytic.
repro.bloom.season 'late_wet' is the nearest existing value: real flowering is Nov-Feb, end of the rains into the early dry season; there is no 'early_dry' value.
photoperiod short_day (threshold 12.0 h) is inferred from the fixed Christmas-season bloom and the genus; not directly documented for this species.
conservation 'not assessed': no IUCN Red List assessment found; the species is widespread and weedy.
Biomes: JUNGLE stands in for 'rainforest margins / mountain forests'; riverbanks and swamps are also recorded but FLOODPLAIN_FOREST/SWAMP are temperate-framed here, so left out.
Range: POWO lists it native south to Bolivia, Paraguay and S Brazil; Wood et al. suggest part of that range is old human introduction. Altitude 0-1100 m (exceptionally 1450 m).
Bark, architecture, growth timings and crop numbers estimated (no published measurements).
Seeds are poisonous; no preparation detail anywhere in the entry.
teonanacatl: Engine has no mushroom shape: entered as shape 'rosette' in the 'ground' category with a 'fungus' block, stage-form 'growth' and no 'fruiting' or 'architecture', exactly as Amanita muscaria in data/biomes/04_taiga.json. A rosette mesh will not read as a thin-stalked bell mushroom.
No biome key for subtropical pine-oak forest or grazed highland pasture: chose CLOUD_FOREST (its edges and clearings) and WET_MEADOW (humid meadows); nothing else on the list fits without overreach.

Altitude: Wikipedia says 'common at 300-550 m (980-1,800 ft)', which looks like a units muddle; the brief's ~1000-1800 m (subtropical montane belt in Guzman's work) is used. No primary source fetched gives the number outright.
Ruin 'maya' rests on the weakest evidence: documented use is Aztec (central Mexico) and Mazatec (Oaxaca); Maya use is only reported (Guatemalan mushroom stones, debated). The rite sentence says so.

mandrake: EGYPT CANNOT GROW IT. Mandrake is not native to Egypt, so a hot-desert Egyptian ruin cannot honestly grow it (HOT_DESERT: temp 18-35 C, moisture 0-0.2, against the plant's cool-wet-winter, summer-dormant Mediterranean band). Sources agree it was introduced to Egypt in the New Kingdom, probably from Canaan and the Levant, and had to be planted in elite gardens with good irrigation (UCM article; Aboelsoud 2010: 'introduced from Canaan and grown locally since the New Kingdom'; egypt-museum.com: 'not native to the Nile Valley itself', seldom thriving in the marshy Nile). So the game needs either a different home world for this plant (MEDITERRANEAN_SCRUB, where the entry lives) or a carried-in plant: found in an irrigated ruin garden, or given by a traveller, never wild in the desert. ruin_compass.json has Egypt unplaced with its biome world open (section FO.9 call 2), so the world pick is Mike's.

NATIVE RANGE IS CONTESTED. Kew POWO accepts M. officinarum narrowly: native N Italy to the NW Balkan Peninsula (the page's own country list names only Italy, Lebanon-Syria and NW Balkans, and contradicts its summary on Lebanon-Syria). POWO gives the wide Mediterranean range (Morocco to Iran, Iberia, Greece, Turkey, Levant) to the autumn-flowering M. autumnalis. Wikipedia and PFAF use the broad sense (the whole Mediterranean). The entry follows the broad sense, as a field guide and the game's 'mediterranean' realm do. Egypt is in neither POWO list in either sense.

WHICH SPECIES IS EGYPT'S? Whether the Egyptian plant (and the mandrake of the Bible and Greek authors) was M. officinarum or M. autumnalis is unsettled: Wikipedia's genus page notes the officinarum/autumnalis split by flowering season (spring vs autumn) and by distribution, and Levant plants are put in autumnalis by Tu et al. 2010. The ruin link is therefore to the genus as much as to this species.

EGYPTIAN EVIDENCE IS ART AND OBJECTS, NOT RITUAL TEXT. Opened sources show the fruit in New Kingdom (mainly 18th Dynasty) banquet and garden scenes (Met: tomb of Nebseny TT 108, c. 1396-1386 BCE, a guest offers another a yellow mandrake fruit; egypt-museum.com: tomb of Nakht TT52), as amulets (Amarna, Swansea Egypt Centre, Gyory 1998: every fifth vegetable amulet in Amarna's North Suburb), faience beads (Amenhotep III), the Mandrake and Lotus Broad Collar (Amarna), plaster at Amarna, and in tomb contexts (UCM article: pectorals of Nefertiti and Tutankhamun, baskets in Tutankhamun's tomb, a jar from the tomb of Maya). Its stated meaning is love, desire, fertility and renewal. No source opened gives a written ritual for it, so sacred.confidence and ceremonial are 'estimated'.

THE BRIEF'S EBERS CLAIM IS NOT CONFIRMED. I could not verify that the Ebers Papyrus lists mandrake. Wikipedia's Ebers Papyrus page does not mention mandrake in its list of plants; Aboelsoud 2010 mentions mandrake only as an imported plant (aphrodisiac; with alcohol, induced unconsciousness) and does not tie it to the Ebers; the UCM article cites the Leiden papyrus (not the Ebers) for a mandrake-and-wine sleep preparation and the Ebers for lotus. Only egypt-museum.com ('The Secret Language of Flowers', uncited popular site) says an Ebers remedy mixes lotus, honey and mandrake; treat that as unverified. I did not open the papyrus or a translation (Manniche, Bardinet, Nunn). Medical use is left out of the rite sentence on purpose.

THE BRIEF'S 'HELD TO THE NOSE BESIDE LOTUS AND POPPIES' IS ONLY PARTLY SUPPORTED. Sources confirm banquet guests hold and offer the mandrake fruit alongside lotus blossoms they sniff; none says the mandrake itself is held to the nose, and none mentions poppies with it (egypt-museum.com says outright that its article does not mention poppies). Not claimed in the entry.

EUROPEAN FOLKLORE (kept out of the rite; Egypt is the ruin): the root often looks like a human figure and was made into amulets for luck and to cure sterility; it was said to scream when pulled from the ground and kill whoever heard it, so people tied roots to animals and had the animal pull them up; pulling it was said to condemn the puller to hell; Dioscorides named 'male' and 'female' mandrakes; the root was used as an anaesthetic in surgery in ancient times (Wikipedia Mandrake (plant), citing Grieve 1931; Roman use cited to Eger et al. 2013, Stolberg 2016). Medieval and later, not Egyptian.

jimsonweed: NATIVE RANGE IS UNSETTLED, AND THE SOURCES DISAGREE. Kew POWO accepts the species as native to Mexico only and lists every US state (Alabama, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas...) as introduced; bplant.org: 'The exact native range of this species is not known' and 'generally agreed to be native to Mexico', some saying Texas; Weakley's Flora (via namethatplant.net): 'non-native? presumably introduced from Mexico or Central America' before 1492; Tennessee-Kentucky Plant Atlas: 'Not Native'; Kansas Wildflowers: 'Native'; Virginia Museum of Natural History: 'likely in Eastern North America before the arrival of Europeans', origin Mesoamerican and spread by people; King et al. 2018: 'its natural range is difficult to determine because it has become so widespread'. realm 'nearctic' and origin 'Mexico (disputed); weed of E US' follow the sources' middle; if the realm gate treats Mexico as another realm, set it by hand. Whether it grew in the Mississippian Southeast before 1492 is open.

THE ARCHAEOLOGY NAMES THE GENUS, NOT THE SPECIES. King et al. 2018 identified atropine, which the authors take as a Datura biomarker ('no other plants in North and Central America are known to contain these alkaloids together'); only atropine was found, no scopolamine. Neither text I read (King et al. in full but its last 210 characters; Lambert et al. abstract page only) names Datura stramonium, D. wrightii, D. inoxia or D. quercifolia. So the link from these vessels to jimsonweed is by region and by the genus, not proven. King et al. report archaeological Datura seeds in Mississippian contexts (AD 1100-1200) in Illinois, none from the Southeast.

THE VESSELS ARE NOT FROM THE GULF SOUTH. The residue finds are from Arkansas (Central Arkansas River valley; Mississippian and Caddoan Mississippian pottery, AD 1400-1700 in King et al.; 'Late Precolumbian' in Lambert et al.). King et al.'s vessels were bought by dealers for the Gilcrease Museum in the early twentieth century, so their find places are poorly documented. Nothing I opened ties Datura to Moundville or Poverty Point (ruin_compass analogues for gulf_swamp); Poverty Point is far older. The ruin link is regional and by analogy, as with the pueblo entry.

THE 'HUNCHBACK CRONE EFFIGY POTS' CLAIM IS UNVERIFIED (it came from a voice chat). What the papers do say: King et al. found atropine in a female effigy bottle from Arkansas (Gilcrease GM 5425-1514) and write that it is 'a cognate of historic-period earth mother figures such as Old-Woman-Who-Never-Dies'; the human-head effigy bottle was also positive. The text I read contains no hunchback or humpback figure and does not call the female figure a crone. Lambert et al.'s abstract page does not mention effigies; its reference list has two Old Woman titles (Baker 1994; Duncan & Diaz-Granados 2004) that I could not read. So only 'a Datura-positive female effigy bottle linked by the authors to an earth-mother figure' is in the entry; the hunchback and the crone are not claimed.

WHAT I COULD NOT READ. The last 210 characters of King et al. 2018. The full text of Lambert et al. 2022 (abstract page only, so its bottle dates, methods and Mississippian comparison are not in the entry, and I did not use its other reported details). The user brief named Tushingham as the author of the absorbed-residue paper; the Cambridge page lists King, Powis, Cheong, Deere, Pickering, Singleton and Gaikwad (Powis is a co-author, Tushingham is not). Per design §FM.9 the entry gives no preparation: the abstract's account of how the disks in the bottles were used to make the drink is left out, only the title is cited.

OTHER RITE EVIDENCE IS WEAK AND NOT CLAIMED. Wikipedia lists Algonquian and Cherokee among peoples who used 'Datura plants' in ceremonies, naming no species, rite or source. The Powhatan huskanaw (Beverley 1705) is Virginia, not the Gulf, and Beverley's own text never names Datura: the Virginia Museum of Natural History page says Schultes and Hofmann 'suspected' Datura in the 'wysoccan' and calls the evidence 'very limited and anecdotal'; Henricus says 'possibly jimsonweed'. The USDA Forest Service ethnobotany page for Datura does not describe Indigenous eastern ritual use of D. stramonium, only the 1676 Jamestown soldiers' poisoning and Shaker adverts.
